row.basis: na'budu; Hebrew la'avod; walk all his ways
row.note: Joshua joins serving YHWH with walking all his ways; Hebrew avad is cognate with the commentary's na'budu, making its service-and-road equation concrete.

row.basis: obey, be my people, walk the commanded way
row.note: Jeremiah makes obedience and walking the commanded way the condition of belonging to God, clarifying the commentary's owned servant who addresses the true master.

row.basis: Abraham goes onward to worship
row.note: Abraham's worship is expressed as a journey with a promised return, a precise counterpart to the commentary's claim that worship and the traversed way are one action.

row.basis: level path of your feet
row.note: Proverbs tells the walker to level the track under his feet, directly supplying the commentary's image of feet making a road surface straight and firm.

row.basis: prepare YHWH's way; make a highway straight
row.note: Isaiah's prepared, straight desert highway gives a scriptural form to the requested sirat as a route made ready for the divine encounter.

row.basis: Way of Holiness; walkers do not go astray
row.note: The highway is explicitly contrasted with going astray, matching the commentary's straight communal road and its lost alternative.

row.basis: this is the way; walk in it; right or left
row.note: A guiding voice gives the traveller the exact formula and directional correction developed in the commentary's guide who goes before the wayfarer.

row.basis: led by streams on a straight, non-stumbling path
row.note: Jeremiah combines a gathered people, water, divine leading, a straight path, and freedom from stumbling in one verse.

row.basis: continual guidance, thirst satisfied, watered garden
row.note: Isaiah binds guidance to provision in dry ground, closely meeting the commentary's route, water, need, and nurturing Lord.

row.basis: make me know your ways; teach me your paths
row.note: This direct prayer for taught paths is a close liturgical companion to ihdina al-sirat.

row.basis: instruct and teach the way to go
row.note: The speaker promises personal instruction and counsel about a particular way, giving a biblical analogue to the hadi who guides a traveller.

row.basis: hand leads and right hand holds
row.note: The psalm makes being led and physically held together, illuminating the commentary's traveller supported while he walks.

row.basis: I hold your right hand; I help you
row.note: YHWH's direct promise to hold the hand and help gives concrete form to the worshipper's request for assistance.

row.basis: teach me to do your will; lead me on level ground
row.note: Prayer for obedience and for the good Spirit to lead on level ground links voluntary service, help, and an upright route.

row.basis: for your name's sake lead and guide me
row.note: The psalm joins the divine name to being led and guided, sharpening the commentary's movement from a naming sign to a requested way.

row.basis: build up the highway; lift a signal for peoples
row.note: Isaiah places a raised signal and a cleared communal road in the same command, matching the commentary's opening sign and constructed path.

row.basis: YHWH's house, taught ways, walked paths
row.note: The nations go to a house so that they may learn and walk God's paths, giving the commentary's road both a community and a destination.

row.basis: level ground so Israel may walk safely
row.note: Baruch makes the leveling of mountains and valleys serve Israel's safe walking, a close late-Jewish parallel to the straight road's communal movement.

row.basis: trees shade Israel at God's command
row.note: The commanded shade gives a direct textual companion to the commentary's road, water, and shade cluster.

row.basis: God leads Israel with mercy and righteousness
row.note: The closing promise combines divine leading, a people on the move, mercy, and righteousness in the terms developed around rahim and guidance.

row.basis: trust, help, make your ways straight
row.note: Sirach joins reliance on God, promised help, and straightened ways in a compact form that closely mirrors the fifth and sixth ayat's prayer.

row.basis: bless God and ask that your ways be made straight
row.note: Tobit's instruction makes blessing the Lord and asking for straight paths one devotional practice, matching the commentary's praise-to-guidance movement.

row.basis: ways of truth and perversity; peace or wrath
row.note: The Rule of the Community develops two opposed ways whose outcomes are peace or divine wrath, supplying a precise Second Temple counterpart to the two faces of losing the path.

row.basis: two ways of life and death
row.note: The opening Two Ways instruction gives a Christian communal formulation for the commentary's straight route and its opposed lost route.

row.basis: YHWH goes before to lead them by the way
row.note: The pillar goes before Israel specifically in order to lead them on the journey, a direct analogue for the guide preceding the traveller.

row.basis: God goes before to find a place to camp
row.note: Deuteronomy depicts God travelling ahead to locate the people's resting place, adding a destination to the commentary's forward-leading guide.

row.basis: take my yoke; learn from me; find rest
row.note: Jesus turns the animal yoke into willing discipleship and rest, directly meeting the commentary's tamed servant and weary traveller.

row.basis: my yoke is easy and my burden light
row.note: The easy yoke and light burden give a concrete Christian counterpart to submissive service that does not crush the one who seeks help.

row.basis: make straight paths for your feet; the lame be healed
row.note: The command retains both the physical track made by feet and the contrast of injury with restored upright movement.

row.basis: guide our feet into the way of peace
row.note: Zechariah's hymn gives the guide the precise task of directing feet into a saving way.

row.basis: narrow way leading to life
row.note: The contrast of a life-giving way with another route gives an explicit Christian form to the commentary's road with two divergent endings.

row.basis: forsook the straight way and went astray
row.note: Second Peter uses the paired language of a straight way and straying, directly matching the commentary's upright walker and dallin.

row.basis: Father's house as destination
row.note: Jesus describes the Father's house as the destination prepared for his people, illuminating the commentary's road that has a final home.

row.basis: I am the way to the Father
row.note: The way is identified with the mediator who brings people to the Father, a direct Christian meeting of route, guide, and home.

row.basis: kept from stumbling and made to stand
row.note: Jude pairs divine preservation from falling with standing before glory, exactly reversing the commentary's falling under wrath.

row.basis: serve not for the sake of reward
row.note: Avot distinguishes service for reward from service freely given to the master, clarifying the commentary's contrast between coerced slavery and chosen worship.

row.basis: freed from sin and enslaved to God
row.note: Paul's paradox of liberation into God's service gives a sharp Christian analogue to voluntary servitude under the true owner.

row.basis: free people, yet servants of God
row.note: The verse expressly holds freedom and God's service together, directly illuminating the commentary's freely chosen kul.

row.basis: Israelites are my servants, brought from Egypt
row.note: Leviticus opposes Egyptian bondage to belonging as God's servants; Hebrew avadim is cognate with Arabic abd and makes the true-owner contrast explicit.

row.basis: Egyptians ruthlessly made Israel serve
row.note: Exodus supplies the forced enslavement that the commentary sets against Moses's willing service to the real Rabb.

row.basis: Israel is God's firstborn son
row.note: Calling enslaved Israel God's son places divine parenthood over Pharaoh's claimed control, sharpening the false-nurturer and true-Rabb contrast.

row.basis: Moses's mother nurses him for Pharaoh's daughter
row.note: Where the Qur'anic Pharaoh presents upbringing as a claim upon Moses, Exodus makes his own mother the nurse and Pharaoh's daughter the payer.

row.basis: Pharaoh's daughter takes and names Moses
row.note: Exodus assigns adoption and naming to Pharaoh's daughter, a significant alternative to Pharaoh himself claiming to have reared Moses in his household.

row.basis: Pharaoh's daughter takes Moses and raises him
row.note: Stephen retells the royal adoption in the same terms that frame the commentary's Pharaoh-and-Moses dispute.

row.basis: Moses refuses to be called Pharaoh's daughter's son
row.note: Hebrews interprets Moses's adult choice as rejection of the royal identity, reinforcing the commentary's contrast of imposed palace status and chosen allegiance.

row.basis: Moses flees to Midian and sits by a well
row.note: The verse fixes the journey and the well that the commentary gathers into Moses's guided road-and-water scene.

row.basis: Midian's daughters draw water and fill troughs
row.note: The source scene explicitly joins the well, women drawing water, and troughs for a flock.

row.basis: Moses helps the women and waters their flock
row.note: Moses's intervention at the well culminates in watering another's flock, the direct biblical parallel to the commentary's scene.

row.basis: the women return to their father's house
row.note: The return home after the well episode adds the household destination that the commentary gives to the road and sacrificial herd.

row.basis: camels kneel by a well as women come to draw water
row.note: The servant's journey joins camel, well, water, and a household-seeking mission in a single scene.

row.basis: Rebekah draws water for the camels
row.note: Water is given to the traveller's animals as well as the traveller, a close counterpart to herd, need, and guidance meeting at the well.

row.basis: YHWH led me on the way to my master's kin
row.note: The servant explicitly credits God with leading him on a route to a household, closely matching guide, owner, way, and home.

row.basis: Jacob rolls the stone and waters Laban's flock
row.note: Jacob's well scene conjoins a journeying relative, water, a flock, and movement into a household as Moses's Midian scene does.

row.basis: water for feet and rest under a tree
row.note: Abraham's hospitality gives travelling visitors water and shade, an exact meeting of two images developed in the commentary.

row.basis: Abraham takes a tender calf from the herd
row.note: The animal from the herd is selected for a household offering of hospitality, paralleling the commentary's separated herd-animal brought to a home.

row.basis: Abraham serves food under the tree
row.note: Serving guests under shade joins willing service, food, and shelter in the Abrahamic setting beside the commentary's route-and-need imagery.

row.basis: Judge of all the earth does justice
row.note: Abraham's appeal to the Judge of all the earth gives a biblical analogue to Rabb al-alamin and the day when justice is rendered.

row.basis: I am dust and ashes before the Lord
row.note: Abraham's self-description before judgment supplies a concrete biblical face-to-dust counterpart to the commentary's humiliated, fallen side of the day.

row.basis: God will provide the lamb for the offering
row.note: Abraham's answer makes the sacrificial animal God's provision, linking herd, divine name, and the journey to worship.

row.basis: Jesus, wearied by travel, sits at Jacob's well
row.note: The scene makes a tired traveller, a road, and a well coincide, closely matching the commentary's Moses cluster.

row.basis: YHWH is my shepherd; I lack nothing
row.note: The shepherd relation gives the herd a known owner whose care answers the commentary's ownerless animal and needy traveller.

row.basis: green pasture and waters of rest
row.note: The shepherd's grazing place and waters give a close biblical form to the flock's going out and returning around water.

row.basis: he leads me in right paths
row.note: The same shepherd restores and guides on right paths, fusing herd leadership and the straight road.

row.basis: shepherd gathers, carries, and gently leads the flock
row.note: The tender leader of the flock gives a strong counterpart to hadi as both guide and herd-leader.

row.basis: no hunger or thirst; guide them to springs
row.note: The promised guide supplies water and relief from need, directly meeting the commentary's travel, thirst, and leading.

row.basis: unknown owner, animal kept at home until restored
row.note: The law expressly imagines not knowing an animal's owner and bringing it home until it can be returned, a close legal counterpart to the ownerless camel.

row.basis: lost sheep; seek your servant
row.note: The speaker is simultaneously a strayed sheep and God's servant who asks to be sought, tightly joining dallin, herd, and worship.

row.basis: lost sheep led astray by their shepherds
row.note: Jeremiah's people are lost sheep whose leaders turned them from their resting place, directly meeting wrong guidance, herd, and home.

row.basis: seek lost, bring back strayed, bind injured
row.note: The divine shepherd's actions reverse loss, falling, and weakness in the terms developed across the commentary's way and herd images.

row.basis: shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out
row.note: The sheep's known name, owner, and being led out directly counter the commentary's animal whose master is unknown.

row.basis: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow his voice
row.note: The shepherd's going before the flock is a precise Christian analogue to the guide ahead of both traveller and herd.

row.basis: I know my own and my own know me
row.note: Mutual recognition between shepherd and sheep intensifies the commentary's final contrast between known ownership and the animal cut off from its owner.

row.basis: seek the one lost sheep until he finds it
row.note: The search for the strayed sheep gives the commentary's lost animal a returning shepherd and a deliberate homeward movement.

row.basis: straying sheep returned to Shepherd and Overseer
row.note: First Peter explicitly turns straying into return to a shepherd, a direct Christian parallel to dallin and guided recovery.

row.basis: sheep without a shepherd
row.note: Jesus reads an unguided crowd through the exact herd-and-leader image the commentary develops for hadi.

row.basis: the Lamb shepherds and guides to springs
row.note: The Lamb who is also shepherd fuses sacrificial animal, herd leader, and water-guidance in an eschatological form.

row.basis: all who enter the world pass before God for judgment
row.note: The Mishnah makes universal judgment resemble a passing flock, closely joining the commentary's herd image to the day of reckoning.

row.basis: horse or mule restrained by bit and bridle
row.note: The psalm's undisciplined animal needing restraint provides a direct counter-image to the commentary's tamed camel and willing servant.

row.basis: YHWH is shade at your right hand
row.note: The divine keeper as shade on the traveller's side gives a compact biblical counterpart to the commentary's shade and sustaining help.

row.basis: clouds, rain, and grass on the hills
row.note: The psalm explicitly has God nourish vegetation through cloud and rain, matching the commentary's nourishing Rabb.

row.basis: rain, fruitful seasons, food from heaven
row.note: Paul's speech identifies the Creator through rain, crops, and food, a close Christian counterpart to the commentary's clouds and plants nourished by the Rabb.

row.basis: Hebrew rachem, womb, and compassion
row.note: Isaiah joins a nursing child, a mother's womb, and rachem; that Hebrew root is cognate with the commentary's rahim and supplies its maternal-mercy image.

row.basis: my name forever; my memorial for generations
row.note: God's self-naming gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's beginning with a name that identifies the owner.

row.basis: called by name; you are mine
row.note: Being called by name and declared God's own directly answers the commentary's contrast between recognized ownership and the masterless animal.

row.basis: put my name on Israel and bless them
row.note: The priestly formula treats the divine name as a mark of belonging and blessing, illuminating name, sign, and completed favor.

row.basis: bring offerings to the place where YHWH's name dwells
row.note: The verse brings sacrifice, divine name, and a chosen dwelling together, closely matching the commentary's herd-animal, spoken name, and home.

row.basis: lamb taken according to each household
row.note: The Passover instruction joins a selected flock-animal to a household, offering a concrete biblical counterpart to sacrifice brought home.

row.basis: luminaries for signs and seasons
row.note: Genesis calls the heavenly lights signs rather than gods, directly serving the commentary's distinction between a sign and what it signifies.

row.basis: Abraham looks at counted stars as promised descendants
row.note: Genesis gives Abraham's star-gazing a covenantal meaning rather than a test of a celestial lord, a meaningful alternative to the commentary's night scene.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars must not be bowed to or served
row.note: The warning against serving the host of heaven is a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary's sun-worshippers who mistake sign for Rabb.

row.basis: sun shining and moon moving in splendor
row.note: Job names the very visual appeal of sun and moon that makes the commentary's ascending celestial signs a test of discernment.

row.basis: heart secretly enticed; hand kissed in worship
row.note: The next verse identifies the move from seeing luminaries to idolatrous devotion, making explicit the error the commentary assigns to sun-worship.

row.basis: sun, moon, stars, and heavenly lights treated as gods
row.note: Wisdom lists the celestial bodies people mistake for rulers of the world, an unusually close Jewish parallel to the commentary's Abrahamic scene.

row.basis: creator perceived from the greatness of created things
row.note: The argument from visible beauty to the Maker directly articulates the commentary's rule that a sign is not the thing it signals.

row.basis: host of heaven worships its maker
row.note: Nehemiah reverses astral worship: the heavenly host itself worships YHWH, so celestial things become servants rather than lords.

row.basis: people worship the sun toward the east
row.note: Ezekiel supplies a concrete scene of sun worship, the precise failure the commentary describes when rising things are treated as Rabb.

row.basis: heavens declare God's glory
row.note: The heavens function as proclamation of God rather than as God, giving a concise biblical form to the sign-and-signified distinction.

row.basis: served the creature rather than the Creator
row.note: Paul makes the inversion of worship explicit, directly matching the commentary's warning against taking a created heavenly sign for its Lord.

row.basis: earth, sea, sky, sun, moon, and stars say they are not God
row.note: Augustine stages the commentary's distinction in first-person form: visible creatures direct the seeker beyond themselves to their maker.

row.basis: YHWH our judge, lawgiver, king, and savior
row.note: Isaiah gathers judge and king in one confession; Hebrew melek is cognate with the commentary's Malik, while the verse joins ownership to deliverance.

row.basis: wicked will not stand in the judgment
row.note: Hebrew qum, to stand, is cognate with the commentary's qama, and the verse places that standing exactly in the judgment scene.

row.basis: Aramaic dina, court seated, books opened
row.note: Daniel's Aramaic dina is cognate with the commentary's din; court, books, and the assembled host make its day-of-reckoning image especially close.

row.basis: Hebrew yadin judges the world in righteousness
row.note: The Hebrew d-y-n verb gives the dīn root a judicial use while its object is the whole world, matching din and alamin.

row.basis: weighed in balances and found lacking
row.note: Daniel turns the balance into a verdict on a king, directly meeting the commentary's scale and judgment-day imagery.

row.basis: just balances and just weights
row.note: The Torah's command makes an unbent balance an ethical demand, supplying the legal ground for the commentary's warning about deficient measure.

row.basis: false balance and just weight
row.note: The proverb sets deceitful scale against the weight God delights in, sharpening the commentary's moral reading of the mizan.

row.basis: make the ephah small and the shekel great; falsify scales
row.note: Amos supplies the concrete market fraud behind the commentary's scene of those who cheat in measure before the Lord of worlds.

row.basis: let God weigh me in just balances
row.note: Job asks for divine weighing that will disclose integrity, directly pairing balance with the final moral account.

row.basis: measured waters and heavens; weighed mountains in scales
row.note: Isaiah places sky, waters, and scales in one divine act, a close counterpart to the commentary's meeting of heaven and balance.

row.basis: all things arranged by measure, number, and weight
row.note: Wisdom makes cosmic order a matter of measure and weight, directly enlarging the commentary's scale from commerce to the worlds.

row.basis: deed written, sealed, witnessed, and weighed out
row.note: Jeremiah's purchase preserves writing, seal, witnesses, money, and duration together, closely paralleling the commentary's debt-document scene.

row.basis: two or three witnesses establish a matter
row.note: The law's witnesses make a legal matter stand, directly illuminating the commentary's witness, forgetting, and uprightly established writing.

row.basis: credit, open ledger, writing hand, collectors, true judgment
row.note: Avot's shop-and-ledger parable unites debt, recorded accounts, payment, and a true judgment in the exact cluster developed in the commentary.

row.basis: three books opened at the new-year judgment
row.note: The Talmud's books for righteous, wicked, and intermediate persons make the judgment day an explicit written accounting.

row.basis: some awaken to life and some to shame
row.note: Daniel's resurrection divides the outcome of the final scene into honor and shame, matching the commentary's contrasting faces on the day.

row.basis: wise shine like the brightness of the sky
row.note: The shining righteous after judgment supplies a biblical counterpart to the softened or radiant face set against dust and disgrace.

row.basis: righteous stand with great confidence
row.note: The righteous standing before their former oppressors closely matches the commentary's upright figure set against those who fall under wrath.

row.basis: they go astray in heart and do not know my ways
row.note: The psalm explicitly combines straying, ignorance of God's ways, and the divine response later called wrath.

row.basis: in my wrath they shall not enter my rest
row.note: The oath of wrath gives the opposite destination to the guided flock's place of rest.

row.basis: way of wicked is darkness; they do not know what makes them stumble
row.note: Proverbs makes lost direction visible as a walker who stumbles without knowing why, closely matching the commentary's fallen wayfarer.

row.basis: crooked paths; walkers do not know peace
row.note: Isaiah's crooked paths and absence of peace provide a direct Hebrew-Bible counterpart to the commentary's route that bends away from guidance.

row.basis: day of wrath and righteous judgment
row.note: Paul's phrase directly joins wrath to an appointed judicial day, the pair the commentary gathers around din.

row.basis: God fixed a day to judge the inhabited world
row.note: Paul's Areopagus speech gives the judgment day a universal scope, closely corresponding to the Lord of the worlds.

row.basis: all appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive what is due
row.note: The verse treats final judgment as recompense owed, a precise Christian counterpart to din as a day of settled debt.

row.basis: dead stand, books open, judged by recorded deeds
row.note: Revelation combines standing persons, opened books, and individual judgment, the central visual cluster of the commentary's day.

row.basis: hide from the face of the enthroned one and the Lamb's wrath
row.note: The terrified call for mountains to fall over them gives an exact Christian image of wrath, faces, and falling.

row.basis: the great day of wrath has come; who can stand
row.note: The verse explicitly sets wrath's day against the ability to stand, matching the commentary's fall-versus-upright contrast.

row.basis: all nations gathered and separated as sheep from goats
row.note: The final judgment is staged as a shepherd's sorting of animals, directly meeting herd imagery and the day of account.

row.basis: sheep on the right and goats on the left
row.note: The bodily arrangement of the flock makes the judgment's two outcomes spatial, complementing the commentary's two ways of being lost.

row.basis: cursed depart into eternal fire
row.note: The king's adverse verdict supplies an explicit Christian judgement-and-wrath counterpart to the angry path's end.

row.basis: stand upright and lift your heads at redemption
row.note: Jesus's command gives the positive posture opposed to the commentary's face-down falling under wrath.

row.basis: they always go astray and have not known my ways
row.note: Hebrews carries the Psalm's language of straying and unknown ways into a Christian warning.

row.basis: they shall not enter my rest in my wrath
row.note: The next verse retains wrath and denied rest, sharpening the commentary's opposed destinations.

row.basis: the measure used is measured back
row.note: The same measure becomes judicial reciprocity, a compact Christian counterpart to balance and account.

row.basis: give account on the day of judgment
row.note: Jesus explicitly uses the language of rendering an account on the final day, closely meeting the commentary's debt-and-record imagery.

row.basis: a king settles accounts with his servants
row.note: The parable puts king, servants, debt, and reckoning in one scene, directly paralleling Malik, abd, and the day debt is closed.

row.basis: settle with an accuser while on the way to the magistrate
row.note: Luke makes the road itself the place to resolve a debt before judgment, an unusually close meeting of path, debt, and day.

row.basis: record of debt with legal demands erased
row.note: Paul's cancelled written debt gives a precise Christian analogue to the commentary's written obligation and its final settlement.

row.basis: each gives an account of himself to God
row.note: The individual account to God directly maps the commentary's day when every person stands before the Lord of worlds.

row.basis: black horse holds a balance scale
row.note: The apocalyptic balance makes measure part of a judgment sequence, extending the commentary's mizan into a Christian final-day image.

row.basis: our Father; hallowed be your name
row.note: The Lord's Prayer opens with a named, direct address to God, closely accompanying the commentary's movement from divine name to second-person devotion.

row.basis: give us today our daily bread
row.note: The shared prayer moves from address to requested provision, matching the commentary's needy traveller and nurturing Lord.

row.basis: forgive us our debts
row.note: The petition uses debt to name what requires divine resolution, directly accompanying the commentary's din-and-borrowing imagery.

row.basis: do not lead us into trial; deliver us from evil
row.note: The final petition asks not to be led into a destructive course and for rescue, closely paralleling help and the requested right way.

row.basis: God's servants worship before the throne
row.note: The final city presents uncoerced service before the true ruler, a culminating Christian counterpart to na'budu.

row.basis: they see his face and bear his name
row.note: The named servants see God's face in the final home, reversing the commentary's faceless loss, wrath, and unknown ownership.

row.basis: distinguish one who serves God from one who does not
row.note: Malachi makes service to God the criterion separating two destinies as judgment approaches, closely matching the commentary's willing servant and two outcomes.

row.basis: children enslaved because of debt
row.note: Nehemiah joins debt to forced enslavement in a concrete social scene, illuminating the commentary's juxtaposition of debt and coerced servitude.

row.basis: I will lead slowly according to the livestock's pace
row.note: Jacob's journey places a leader ahead of children and nursing flocks, supplying a specific pastoral bridge to the commentary's guide, herd, and tired traveller.

row.basis: living water given at the well
row.note: At the traveller's well, water becomes a divine gift; this extends the commentary's physical water-and-need scene into John's symbolic register.

row.basis: the community called the Way
row.note: Acts turns a communal allegiance into the name of a way, a specific but non-narrative counterpart to the commentary's path joined to a people.

row.basis: benei maron read through sheep or a narrow pass
row.note: The Talmud's interpretations of the Mishnah's procession make individual passage before the judge resemble either a flock or a constricted route, joining herd, path, and judgment.

row.basis: Abraham's anti-idol argument in Terah's workshop
row.note: The midrash recasts Abraham's discernment of false gods as a contest with made images, extending the commentary's sign-versus-Lord distinction.

row.basis: Abraham teaches one creator rather than celestial powers
row.note: Josephus interprets Abraham as arguing from the ordered cosmos to one creator, a close historical reception of the commentary's astral scene.

row.basis: Moses refuses Egyptian nurses and is nursed by his mother
row.note: The tradition makes Pharaoh's household dependent on Moses's own mother for his nurture, intensifying the commentary's challenge to Pharaoh's claim of upbringing.

row.basis: Moses thought his brothers would understand his deliverance
row.note: Stephen supplies a positive intention for Moses's intervention among the oppressed, an interpretive counterpoint to the commentary's self-description as among the lost.

row.basis: Wisdom enters the servant of the Lord against dread kings
row.note: Wisdom portrays Moses as God's servant confronting royal power, giving a late-Jewish bridge between the commentary's true Rabb and Pharaoh's coercion.

row.basis: records, weighing, and judgment of souls
row.note: The apocalypse's judgment tableau gathers written records, scales, and verdicts, a close later-Jewish expansion of the commentary's balance-and-account scene.

row.basis: look to him, become radiant, faces not ashamed
row.note: The psalm's radiant, unashamed faces give a specific positive counterpart to the commentary's contrasting faces, though outside its final-judgment setting.

row.basis: no one can serve two masters
row.note: Jesus's master-servant saying supplies a focused Christian bridge between worship, ownership, and the commentary's contrast of true and false masters.

row.basis: offering drawn from cattle or flock
row.note: Leviticus supplies the sacrificial category of herd and flock behind the commentary's animal separated for an offering, without its full homeward scene.

row.basis: root of Jesse as a signal sought by nations
row.note: The raised signal draws a people toward a resting place, a secondary biblical bridge to the commentary's sign, path, and communal destination.

row.basis: rahum, mercy, and slow anger
row.note: YHWH proclaims himself compassionate and slow to anger; Hebrew rahum shares the r-h-m root with the commentary's rahim and directly sets mercy beside wrath.

row.basis: father's compassion for children
row.note: Psalm 103 uses the r-h-m root for a father's compassion toward children, adding a paternal form to the commentary's nurturing Rabb and rahim.

row.basis: wandered without a way to an inhabited city
row.note: The psalm begins with people lost on a desert route and unable to find a city to dwell in, closely matching the commentary's road without its final home.

row.basis: hungry, thirsty, and fainting on the way
row.note: The travellers' thirst and failing strength give a direct biblical counterpart to the weary wayfarer who asks the Rabb for help.

row.basis: led by a straight way to a city to dwell in
row.note: YHWH leads the lost travellers on a straight way to habitation, combining guidance, road, and house in the commentary's exact sequence.

row.basis: lead the blind by an unknown way and make crooked places straight
row.note: Isaiah's guide leads those who do not know the route and straightens its crooked parts, directly reversing the commentary's dallin.

row.basis: an angel guards the way and brings Israel to a prepared place
row.note: The messenger goes before Israel to protect the road and bring them to a destination, giving a close biblical form to the helper-guide and final home.

row.basis: leader goes out before the people so they are not sheep without a shepherd
row.note: Moses asks for a leader who goes before and leads the congregation, explicitly joining the traveller-guide and herd-leader images.

row.basis: the breaker and king go before the people
row.note: Micah imagines a path opened and a king going at the people's head, a strong counterpart to the commentary's guide who precedes the community.

row.basis: YHWH goes before and is Israel's rear guard
row.note: The divine escort ahead and behind gives a precise scriptural counterpart to the commentary's traveller held from both sides.

row.basis: lamp for my feet and light for my path
row.note: The word gives a walker light exactly at the feet and on the path, sharpening the commentary's concrete imagery of movement and guidance.

row.basis: the path of the righteous is level
row.note: The upright God makes the righteous person's path level, directly echoing the commentary's uprightness and smoothed road.

row.basis: led his people like sheep and guided them like a flock
row.note: The exodus is described as divine guidance of sheep through the wilderness, fusing route, herd, and true shepherd.

row.basis: livestock led down to rest by YHWH's Spirit
row.note: Isaiah compares the Spirit-led people to livestock brought to rest and connects the leading with God's name, meeting herd, guide, destination, and sign.

row.basis: gathered flock brought to its land and fed
row.note: Ezekiel's shepherd brings scattered sheep home and feeds them on their own land, supplying the return-to-home side of the commentary's herd route.

row.basis: people wander like sheep for lack of a shepherd
row.note: Zechariah states the inverse of the commentary's hadi: sheep wander and suffer when no shepherd leads them.

row.basis: come, worship, bow down, and kneel before the maker
row.note: The psalm gives worship a bodily posture of bending before the creator, a close counterpart to willing, tamed service.

row.basis: people of his pasture and sheep of his hand
row.note: The worshipping people are simultaneously a flock possessed and tended by God, directly answering the commentary's ownerless animal.

row.basis: YHWH raises those bowed down
row.note: The psalm's raising of the bent gives a direct positive counterpart to the commentary's fallen person and its upright walker.

row.basis: God opens Hagar's eyes to a well and gives the child water
row.note: Guidance to a well supplies water in a wilderness crisis, a close parallel to the commentary's path, water, need, and divine provision.

row.basis: Moses brings water from the rock for the thirsty people
row.note: The Exodus water scene gives Moses a second, communal road-and-water episode beside the Midian well developed in the commentary.

row.basis: God leads through dry wilderness and brings water from rock
row.note: Deuteronomy explicitly binds wilderness leading to water for a thirsty people, closely matching the commentary's guided journey and well.

row.basis: a way in wilderness and rivers in desert
row.note: Isaiah places road-making and water-making together in an otherwise impassable land, a direct counterpart to the commentary's path and water.

row.basis: water in wilderness to give drink to God's people
row.note: The water is expressly given for the chosen people's drinking, adding communal provision to the commentary's individual thirsty traveller.

row.basis: waters break out in wilderness and streams in desert
row.note: The water imagery supplies the necessary environmental counterpart to Isaiah's Way of Holiness already relevant to the commentary's straight route.

row.basis: springs sent into valleys to run among mountains
row.note: The creator directs springs through the land, a strong biblical image for water set into a traversable landscape.

row.basis: wild animals drink from the springs
row.note: The springs meet the thirst of animals, directly extending the commentary's convergence of water and herd.

row.basis: grass for livestock and food from the earth
row.note: God's vegetation feeds both livestock and humans, closely matching the commentary's Rabb who nourishes creatures through plant growth.

row.basis: rain waters earth and gives seed and bread
row.note: Rain's passage into growth and food supplies a precise scriptural counterpart to clouds, plants, and completed provision.

row.basis: taught Ephraim to walk and carried him in arms
row.note: Hosea makes God the one who teaches a child to walk and carries him, an especially close true-Rabb counterpart to Pharaoh's claimed upbringing.

row.basis: children raised and brought up, yet rebellious
row.note: Isaiah's parental complaint gives a biblical counterpoint to nurture received as a claim and to the servant who must choose allegiance.

row.basis: a mother comforts her child; God comforts Jerusalem
row.note: The maternal comparison gives rahim's nurturing register a concrete biblical counterpart in divine comfort.

row.basis: ram offered in place of Abraham's son
row.note: The caught ram realizes the sacrificial animal that Abraham said God would provide, adding the herd-animal's actual offering to the journey scene.

row.basis: seek the place where God puts his name to dwell
row.note: The chosen dwelling and its resident name provide the house-and-name side of the sacrificial movement developed in the commentary.

row.basis: words bound as a sign on hand and forehead
row.note: The covenantal sign worn on the body gives a Jewish scriptural counterpart to the commentary's image of name and stamp.

row.basis: a mark set on foreheads before punishment
row.note: Ezekiel joins a distinguishing mark on faces with the approach of judgment, closely meeting the commentary's sign, face, and wrath cluster.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars loved, served, followed, and worshipped
row.note: Jeremiah explicitly combines astral worship with service and following, a very close counterpart to the commentary's celestial false lords and path imagery.

row.basis: do not fear the signs of heaven as the nations do
row.note: Jeremiah joins the heavenly signs to the nations' mistaken way, directly extending the commentary's distinction between sign and Lord.

row.basis: God appoints the sun, moon, and stars for their courses
row.note: The luminaries are governed creations under God's ordinance, a direct counter-narrative to calling them Rabb.

row.basis: sun, moon, and stars praise YHWH
row.note: The celestial bodies are themselves worshippers, reversing the commentary's scene of humans worshipping them.

row.basis: every knee bows and every tongue swears to YHWH
row.note: The universal bodily confession gives a direct biblical form to worship before the sole sovereign.

row.basis: day God rises to gather nations and pour wrath
row.note: Zephaniah combines divine rising, gathered peoples, and poured wrath in a final-day scene beside the commentary's standing and anger imagery.

row.basis: recompense, a slipping foot, and the near day of calamity
row.note: The Song of Moses connects repayment and an imminent day with a foot that slips, closely matching debt, judgment, and falling from the path.

row.basis: though fallen, I rise; darkness becomes light
row.note: Micah gives the commentary's fallen and upright walker an explicit scriptural reversal.

row.basis: first judgment question asks whether business was conducted faithfully
row.note: The Talmud makes honest commercial dealing the first question at judgment, a precise rabbinic bridge between false measure and final account.

row.basis: formed, born, die, and give account before the King of kings
row.note: Avot places unavoidable life and death under a final accounting before the King, tightly joining Malik, din, and personal debt.

row.basis: narrow path to a city between fire and water
row.note: The vision's perilous single route toward an inheritable city makes road, water, danger, and destination a striking Second Temple counterpart to the commentary's way.

row.basis: Moses's generation drinks from the spiritual rock, identified as Christ
row.note: Paul explicitly rereads the wilderness water episode, extending the commentary's Moses-water meeting through a Christian interpretive claim.

row.basis: water becomes a spring to eternal life
row.note: John turns water received at the well into a spring within the receiver, a distinct continuation of the commentary's water-and-need image.

row.basis: the thirsty are invited to come and drink
row.note: Jesus's public invitation makes thirst a route toward divinely given water, closely accompanying the commentary's needy traveller.

row.basis: the thirsty may take the water of life freely
row.note: The final invitation joins thirst, gift, and the completed eschatological home developed at the commentary's road's end.

row.basis: the king receives food and drink given to the needy
row.note: In the judgment scene, service to the hungry and thirsty is received by the king himself, linking need, willing service, and din.

row.basis: present bodies as a living sacrifice in worship
row.note: Paul turns voluntary embodied worship into sacrifice, a direct Christian counterpart to the commentary's chosen servant and offered animal.

row.basis: sacrifice of praise and lips confessing God's name
row.note: The verse makes praise of the divine name a sacrifice, closely joining the commentary's name, praise, and ritual offering.

row.basis: spiritual house, priesthood, and spiritual sacrifices
row.note: First Peter unites house and sacrifice in a worshipping community, providing a Christian counterpart to the commentary's destination-house and sacrificial herd.

row.basis: new and living way opened through the curtain
row.note: The sanctuary is entered by a named living way, a precise Christian meeting of route and the divine house.

row.basis: God brings up the great shepherd of the sheep
row.note: Hebrews names the eschatological shepherd in a covenant setting, directly meeting herd, sacrifice, and true guidance.

row.basis: God equips people to do God's will
row.note: The prayer for divine equipping gives a Christian form to the commentary's servant who asks for help in willing obedience.

row.basis: seal God's servants on their foreheads before harm
row.note: The seal marks divine servants before approaching catastrophe, closely corresponding to the commentary's stamp, ownership, and wrath.

row.basis: the Lord knows those who are his; the foundation bears a seal
row.note: The seal combines known ownership and moral departure from evil, directly reversing the commentary's animal with no known master.

row.basis: one God and one Lord through whom all things are
row.note: In the context of many so-called heavenly gods and lords, Paul names one God and one Lord, closely matching the commentary's rejection of celestial rivals.

row.basis: turn from idols to serve a living and true God
row.note: The conversion formula explicitly combines leaving false objects of service with serving the living true God.

row.basis: creator is Lord of heaven and earth
row.note: Paul names the maker of the world and all it contains as Lord of heaven and earth, a direct Christian counterpart to Rabb al-alamin.

row.basis: fear God, give glory, judgment hour, worship the creator
row.note: This angelic proclamation joins praise, judgment, worship, creation, and springs of water in one unusually close parallel to the commentary's whole movement.

row.basis: righteous shine like the sun in their Father's kingdom
row.note: The final shining of the righteous gives a Christian counterpart to the commentary's contrasting judgment-day faces.

row.basis: Hallelujah: salvation, glory, and power belong to God
row.note: The heavenly acclamation places praise before the declaration of judgment that follows, paralleling the commentary's hamd before the narrated gift.

row.basis: God's judgments are true and just
row.note: Revelation answers the praise with true and just judgment, directly joining hamd, din, and the correction of corrupt judgment.
